snippet.title: Air Crash Investigation - Queens Catastrophe (S13E05) - [FULL EPISODE]
snippet.description:
American Airlines Flight 587 was a regularly scheduled international passenger flight from John F. Kennedy International Airport, New York City, to Las Américas International Airport, Santo Domingo, Dominican Republic. On November 12, 2001, the Airbus A300B4-605R flying the route crashed into the neighborhood of Belle Harbor on the Rockaway Peninsula of Queens, New York City, shortly after takeoff, killing all 251 passengers and 9 crew members aboard, as well as five people on the ground. the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) attributed the disaster to the first officer's overuse of rudder controls in response to wake turbulence from a preceding Japan Airlines Boeing 747-400 that took off minutes before it. According to the NTSB, the aggressive use of the rudder controls by the first officer, the result of a flawed training scenario that overexaggerated the effects of wake turbulence, stressed the vertical stabilizer until the rudder was ripped from the aircraft. The airliner's two engines also separated from the aircraft before impact due to the intense forces.

snippet.title: Stormy Cockpit | Kenya Airways Flight 507 | Air Crash Investigation | National Geographic
snippet.description:
Kenya Airways Flight 507 was a scheduled international passenger service between Abidjan, Ivory Coast, and Nairobi, Kenya with a stopover in Douala, Cameroon, operated by Kenya Airways. On 5 May 2007, the Boeing 737-800 aircraft serving the flight crashed immediately after takeoff from Douala International Airport in Cameroon, killing all 114 occupants onboard.

The plane broke up into small pieces and came to rest mostly submerged in a mangrove swamp, 5.4 kilometers (3.4 mi; 2.9 nmi) to the south (176°) of the end of Douala International Airport's runway 12. There were no survivors. The investigation by the Cameroon Civil Aviation Authority determined that the pilots failed to notice and correct excessive bank following takeoff. This led to the loss of control and crash of the aircraft.

snippet.title: Air Crash Investigation - Deadly Silence (S16E01) - [FULL EPISODE]
snippet.description:
On October 25, 1999, a chartered Learjet 35 business jet was scheduled to fly from Orlando, Florida, United States to Dallas, Texas, United States. Early in the flight, the aircraft, which was climbing to its assigned altitude on autopilot, lost cabin pressure, and all six on board were incapacitated and killed by hypoxia, a lack of oxygen in the brain and body. The aircraft continued climbing past its assigned altitude, then failed to make the westward turn toward Dallas over North Florida and continued on its northwestern course, flying over the Southern and Midwestern United States for almost four hours and 1,500 miles (2,400 km). The plane ran out of fuel over South Dakota and crashed into a field near Aberdeen after an uncontrolled descent. The two pilots were Michael Kling and Stephanie Bellegarrigue. The four passengers on board were PGA Tour golfer Payne Stewart; his agent Robert Fraley (a former Alabama Crimson Tide football team member). snippet.title: Air Crash Investigation - Meltdown over Kathmandu (S21E06) - [FULL EPISODE]
snippet.description:
US-Bangla Airlines Flight 211 was a scheduled international passenger flight from Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport in Dhaka, Bangladesh, to Tribhuvan International Airport in Kathmandu, Nepal, that crashed on 12 March 2018 while landing, killing 51 of the 71 people aboard. The aircraft, a 76-seat Bombardier Q400 operated by US-Bangla Airlines, burst into flames after the crash. The 20 surviving passengers were badly injured from the impact and the fire. A commission appointed by the government of Nepal investigated the accident and concluded that the probable cause of the crash was pilot disorientation and a loss of situational awareness of the flight crew. The report was criticized by the airline and by the Bangladeshi representative on the commission, who felt that the air traffic controllers at Tribhuvan International Airport did not do their job properly and could have prevented the accident.

When an emergency strikes in mid-air, a split-second decision can mean the difference between survival and catastrophe. In this episode, we break down three tragic aviation disasters where highly experienced crews made fatal mistakes under extreme pressure.

Next, we investigate KLM City Hopper Flight 433, where a short circuit caused a false oil pressure warning, prompting the crew to idle a perfectly healthy engine before a fatal go-around attempt. Finally, we go inside the Mojave Desert disaster of Virgin Galactic’s Spaceship 2, which disintegrated just 14 seconds after rocket ignition because a highly decorated test pilot unlocked a critical aerodynamic feathering system early while accelerating toward Mach 3.

Why did the crew ignore multiple warning signs? How did a casual conversation distract them during a critical phase of flight? And could air traffic control have prevented the disaster?

Featuring cockpit voice recordings, accident reconstruction, NTSB findings, and expert analysis, this documentary examines the devastating crash of Comair Flight 5191 and the lessons learned that continue to shape aviation safety today.

snippet.title: Missouri Plane Crash: 12 Dead After Skydiving Aircraft Goes Down Near Butler
snippet.description:
✈️ Missouri Skydiving Plane Crash, The Jump Flight That Never Reached Altitude

In this video, we break down the tragic story of the Butler, Missouri skydiving plane crash, a routine Sunday jump flight that turned into one of the deadliest skydiving aircraft disasters the United States has seen in decades.

The weather was clear.
The winds were light.
The runway was open.
The aircraft had already flown earlier jump runs that morning.

Twelve people lifted off from Butler Memorial Airport, including the pilot and eleven skydivers. For most of them, this was supposed to be another familiar climb to altitude. For two tandem jumpers, it may have been the experience of a lifetime.

But within minutes of takeoff, something went terribly wrong.

The aircraft struggled to climb.
Witnesses say it appeared unable to gain altitude.
The pilot banked left, possibly trying to reach the highway beside the airport.
Then, at low altitude, the plane stalled and crashed into a field near the runway.

All twelve people on board were killed.

How does a purpose-built skydiving aircraft take off on a clear morning and fail to climb?

Was the aircraft losing power?
Was there an engine problem?
Was aircraft loading, maintenance, performance, or another factor involved?

✈️ Usinsk Runway Crisis, The 30 Seconds That Nearly Ended in Disaster

In this video, we break down one of the most intense near-disasters in aviation history, where a Boeing 737 carrying 105 passengers and four fuel-critical MiG-31 fighter jets converged on a single icy runway at Usinsk Airport on November 15, 2018.

The landing was routine.
The runway was not.

Frost reduced braking performance. The Boeing could not clear in time.
And overhead, four military jets were arriving with almost no fuel left.

They could not hold.
They could not go around.
They had one chance.

What followed was not a crash, but something just as dangerous, a complete breakdown in communication between military and civilian aviation systems that pushed multiple aircraft into a no-margin situation.

How do five aircraft end up fighting for one runway?
And how close did this come to a catastrophic collision?

✈️ The Situation

At first, everything looks manageable.

A Boeing 737 lands and begins rollout on a frost-covered runway. Due to reduced braking, it cannot exit as planned and must continue to the far end.

At the same time, four MiG-31 fighter jets are diverting.

But the critical detail is missing.

The civilian controllers are never told these aircraft are fuel-critical. They believe this is a routine diversion.

In reality, at least two jets have no fuel left for another approach.

🔥 The Critical Moment

As the Boeing reaches the runway end, the first MiG lands and stops beside it.

Then the second jet arrives.

ATC issues a go-around.

The pilot refuses.

Not because he wants to, but because he cannot.

That is the moment the situation becomes a real emergency.

Two fighter jets end up parked beside a passenger aircraft, both arriving at the edge of fuel exhaustion, while two more jets are still inbound.

🔥 The Investigation

According to findings from aviation authorities, this incident was not caused by a single failure.

It was a chain of system-level breakdowns:

• Military did not communicate the emergency fuel state
• Civilian ATC treated it as a routine diversion
• No coordination protocol between military and civilian systems
• Multiple aircraft forced into a single runway sequence
• Extreme weather and runway conditions reduced safety margins

There was no collision.

But the event was officially classified as a probable risk of collision, and came dangerously close to becoming something far worse.

On May 17th, 2026, two U.S. Navy EA-18G Growler jets took off from Mountain Home Air Force Base in Idaho during the Gunfighter Skies Air Show.

Thousands of spectators were watching from the ground.
The weather was clear.
The maneuver was planned.
The pilots were highly trained.

Nothing about the performance was supposed to end in disaster.

But in less than three seconds, a precise military demonstration turned into a terrifying emergency.

The two Navy jets made contact in mid-air. Instead of separating, they appeared to lock together, spinning and falling toward the desert floor while four aviators inside the cockpits had only moments to react.

How does a routine air show maneuver turn into a mid-air collision?
Why did the jets stay locked together?
And how did all four crew members manage to eject before impact?

The aircraft involved were EA-18G Growlers, advanced U.S. Navy electronic warfare jets based on the F/A-18F Super Hornet.

In other words, the people flying these aircraft were not inexperienced.

Each jet carried two crew members: a pilot in the front seat and an Electronic Warfare Officer in the rear. Between them, the four aviators had thousands of hours of flying experience and had trained for this kind of demonstration.

But during the Gunfighter Skies Air Show, something went wrong during a close pass.

Video from the crowd captured the moment the two Growlers came together, made contact, and appeared to become tangled in the air. Pieces broke away from the aircraft, and the jets began spinning as one locked mass.

For the crew in the lower aircraft, the situation was especially dangerous.

Ejection seats fire upward. If another aircraft is directly above you, ejecting can be fatal. For several seconds, the bottom crew had almost no safe path out.

Then the aircraft shifted.

A tiny window opened.

And in that moment, all four aviators ejected.

Four parachutes opened above the Idaho desert as the two jets crashed roughly two miles northwest of the base and exploded on impact.

The aircraft were destroyed.
The air show was cancelled.
The base went into lockdown.

But all four crew members survived.

• Did wind gusts affect the formation spacing?

snippet.title: A Critical Mistake Caused This Airport Collision
snippet.description:
A fully operational aircraft.
A stable approach.
A controlled airport environment.

And yet, within seconds of landing, everything went wrong.

At LaGuardia Airport, a passenger jet collided with a fire truck — not because of a single mistake, but because multiple safety systems failed at the exact same moment.

✈️ Incident Overview
• Flight: Air Canada Express AC8646
• Aircraft: Bombardier CRJ900
• Date: March 22, 2026
• Location: LaGuardia Airport (Runway 4), New York
• Conditions: Heavy rain, low visibility
• Passengers & Crew: 76 onboard
• Outcome: Collision with airport fire vehicle during landing✈️ LaGuardia Airport Collision, The System Failures Behind Air Canada 8646

In this video, we break down the shocking and deeply complex events behind the LaGuardia Airport collision, where Air Canada Express Flight AC8646 struck a fire truck during landing on March 22, 2026.

The weather was poor, but within legal limits.
The aircraft was fully functional.
The approach was stable.

Nothing suggested the flight would end in disaster.

Yet within seconds of touchdown, a fire truck entered the runway.
There was no warning to the pilots.
No automated alert.
No time to react.

What followed was a collision that investigators are still trying to fully explain.

There was no engine failure.

snippet.title: Air Crash Investigation - The Final Push (S14E05) - [FULL EPISODE]
snippet.description:
FedEx Express Flight 80 was a scheduled cargo flight from Guangzhou Baiyun International Airport, China, to Narita International Airport, Japan, operated by FedEx Express. At 06:48 JST (UTC+09:00) on March 23, 2009, the McDonnell Douglas MD-11F registered N526FE  operating the flight crashed while attempting a landing on Runway 34L in gusty and highly variable weather conditions, including winds in excess of 40 knots (74 km/h). The aircraft became destabilized after the fatigued co-pilot's delayed start of the landing flare, subsequently exacerbated by his excessively large, nose-down inputs causing abrupt changes in the plane's pitch, increasing the speed and severity of repeated touchdowns during the bounced landing. This resulted in a structural failure of the landing gear and airframe, with the left wing detaching and power of the jet on the right wing thus causing the plane to roll. The plane came to a stop off of the runway, with the plane inverted and on fire. The captain and first officer were the only occupants, and were both killed in the crash. The airport's rescue crew got the pilots out of the aircraft and tried getting them to a hospital, but the crew succumbed to their injuries before they could receive medical attention.
